---
name: work-status
description: 'Reports where the project''s work items stand: progress, blockers, the next item, and decisions waiting on the owner. Use whenever the owner asks about project or item status, even one item, for example "where are we", "what''s next", or "is X done yet". Not for a chat recap; use session-summary.'
---

# Work status

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Reports where the work stands. This skill only reads: apart from the CLI's own sync (the history rows it writes for the owner's hand moves), it never changes an item, memory, or a file.

## Steps

1. Use the project briefing when this conversation has it and nothing changed since. Otherwise run it.
   `toolkit brief`
2. The owner named an item or an area: answer about that item only. Where it stands in plain words, what is done and left in its Roadmap, its blockers, and its next action.
   `toolkit work show <id>`
3. The whole project: read the tree, the recommended next item, the decisions waiting on the owner, and the current focus.
   `toolkit work list --tree`
   `toolkit work next`
   `toolkit work decisions`
   `toolkit memory focus`
4. Answer in the order and shape in "How to answer" below. Say every stage in plain words with the item id ("WI-012 is in testing"); the labels come from the lifecycle.
   `toolkit work lifecycle`
5. For each problem, name the skill that fixes it, without running it: moved or missing items, `work-organize`; setup warnings, `project-setup`; decisions, `work-decide`.
6. "Show the board": local tracker, summarize `.work-items/DASHBOARD.md`; Notion, give the Work Items link (`references/tracker-notion.md`, "The board link").
   `toolkit config get notion.workItems.url`
7. End with one thing the owner can say next, for example "Say 'what do you need from me' to go through the 2 decisions."

## Gotchas

- Run each `toolkit` command alone: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script (in Codex that runs it inside the sandbox, where it fails; `references/toolkit-commands.md`).
- "Agent to-do" lines in the decisions list are the agent's own steps, not decisions. Count and show only the decisions.
- Archived items are hidden from the briefing and the recommended next item. Mention them only when the owner asks.
- GitHub Issues or Jira: `toolkit work` exits with code 3. Read the issues with the tracker's own tool (`references/tracker-github.md` or `references/tracker-jira.md`, section "The `toolkit work` steps") and answer in the same order.
- Nothing is tracked yet: say so in one line and offer `work-on` for the first piece of work.

## How to answer

- Lead with the answer, not with how you found it.
- Decisions first, because only the owner can unblock them: the count, then one line each with the item id, what is being decided, and how long it has waited when the record shows it.
- One line per item in progress: id, title, plain stage, what is left, and who it waits on.
- The recommended next item and why, in one line.
- Recently done: items finished since the last session, when the record shows it. Skip it when there are none.
- Anything moved, renamed, or broken, with the skill that fixes it. Repeat every change the briefing or a `toolkit` command reported ("Re-parented: ...", "Renamed folder: ...", "Changed by hand: ..."), one line each, even when the owner made it himself.
- Keep it short. The owner can ask about one item for detail.

Example:

```markdown
2 decisions wait on you:
- WI-012: approve the CSV export result (waiting since 2026-09-26).
- WI-015: choose design A (built-in report) or B (custom page).

In progress:
- WI-014 "Nightly sync", in build (stage 08): P2 of 3 left; waiting on nobody.

Next: WI-016 "Login page copy", because it blocks the release and needs no decision.

Say "what do you need from me" to go through the 2 decisions.
```

## Not this skill

- "What did we do in this chat": `session-summary`.
- "What do you need from me": `work-decide`, which walks through each decision.
- "What did we decide about X": `memory-find`.

## References

| File | Open it when |
| --- | --- |
| [references/tracker-local.md](references/tracker-local.md) | `tracker.type` is `local`: the dashboard, archived items, hand moves |
| [references/tracker-notion.md](references/tracker-notion.md) | `tracker.type` is `notion`: the board link, cards the owner changed |
| [references/tracker-github.md](references/tracker-github.md) | A `toolkit work` command exits 3 in a GitHub Issues project |
| [references/tracker-jira.md](references/tracker-jira.md) | A `toolkit work` command exits 3 in a Jira project |
| [references/work-item-format.md](references/work-item-format.md) | Reading an item's sections: what each one holds |
| [references/recording-owner-answers.md](references/recording-owner-answers.md) | Stage wording and how to end the reply |
| [references/toolkit-commands.md](references/toolkit-commands.md) | Any `toolkit` command exits with a code other than 0 |

# Humanize Anything Sent to Another Person

Any text that will leave the project and be read by someone other than the owner
is run through the `humanizer` skill before the owner sees the final version.
Use the `unslop` skill when `humanizer` is not installed. That covers emails,
chat messages, support case text and comments, GitHub issues, pull request
descriptions, client documents, and any file made to hand to someone else.

Keep every fact, name, id, number, and date exactly as it was. Write it in the
owner's voice, first person, when it goes out under their name.

It does not apply to chat replies to the owner, work items, project knowledge,
code, or commit messages.
# Keep the Active Work Item Accurate

The work tracker is the source of truth for current work.

- Before substantial work, use the `work-on` skill. Read the active item's requirements, state, next step, and blockers.
- Save the owner's decisions, requirements, and corrections in the item or its linked document before moving on.
- When the work needs the owner's decision, add it to the item's Open Questions with "Decision needed from: owner" and set the item's `waiting_on` to `owner`. The `work-decide` skill records the answer.
- `build` and `data-load` work needs approved requirements before it starts. A later stage does not revoke that approval.
- After the owner accepts agent-led delivery, ask how the team is arranged. That choice authorizes helpers for that goal only.
- Mark an item Done only after the owner approves the result.
- Before ending unfinished work, record the exact next step in the item.

`toolkit work lifecycle` prints the stages, statuses, and approval gates. "Where information goes" in `AGENTS.md` is the routing table; the `work-delegate` skill holds the delivery offer and team questions, and the `handoff` skill holds the handoff steps.
# Review and Save Project Memory

This rule applies to the main agent. The project memory system is chosen at setup and recorded in `.toolkit.json`; with built-in memory it is the local `.memory/` folder. It is the single project memory store. Claude's native auto-memory and the `claude-toolkit` Second Brain plugin are disabled for this project. The session-start briefing shows the current focus in Claude Code and Codex. Do not treat a hook reminder as a save decision.

## Decide the destination first

Read the memory criteria (`.memory/memory-criteria.md` with built-in memory) and the likely owning record. Send the owner's instructions for how the agent works to `.claude/rules/owner-preferences.md` (`toolkit rule add`), never to memory. Send current focuses, owner to-dos, and handoff context to the current focus; sourced terminology to the glossary; qualifying otherwise-unowned durable context to a topic; active work to the chosen tracker; decisions for the whole project to `DECISIONS.md`; accepted delivered behavior to requirements; the technical approach to the design kept with its work item; verified current structure to the System Guide; and repeatable procedure to instructions or a skill. Raw external documentation stays in its source folder. A small memory pointer can route future sessions to a hard-to-find authority without copying its body.

Review on explicit remember/forget requests, corrections, standing preferences, meaningful decisions or discoveries, significant fixes or episodes, people/tool/reference changes, focus shifts, work-item completion, and handoffs. The toolkit's `UserPromptSubmit` hook flags only explicit keep phrases, and its Stop hook checks once per turn that such a phrase was handled. Do not save on every hook reminder or every turn. A review can end with no memory.

## Approval

The `memory-save` skill holds the approval policy: what the owner's own words authorize, what needs a yes in onboarding mode, what trusted mode allows, and what always needs the owner. The mode is `memory.approval` in `.toolkit.json`; only an explicit owner instruction changes it. A yes authorizes the shown operation and meaning only. Silence does not. An unanswered save question is kept as a proposal: the agent does not rely on it, and `work-decide` shows it to the owner until he approves or rejects it. The `memory-save` skill says how.

If the owner says a proposed item should not be memory, withdraw it. Write only a general selection rule, as a rule with `toolkit rule add`, if their feedback supplies one; do not restate the rejected fact in the current focus or another topic. Review similar candidates against that rule from then on.

## Saving and completion

The main agent saves memory itself through the `memory-save` skill, which runs `toolkit memory` commands; there is no curator agent. Search first with `toolkit memory find`, then save with `toolkit memory save`, retire with `toolkit memory retire`, and write the current focus or glossary with `toolkit memory focus --set-file` or `toolkit memory glossary --set-file`. The commands lock memory, refuse stale edits, and rebuild the index.

For a focus-only change or already-authorized glossary maintenance, save without a lasting-memory question. Several independent signals can be grouped into one save; do not run parallel writes against the same topic or index. Before claiming a save succeeded, read it back with `toolkit memory get` and run `toolkit doctor`; tell the user briefly what was retained or what needs a decision.
# Owner Preferences

How the owner wants the agent to work in this project. Follow every line, every session. Each line ends with the date and where the instruction came from. Change this file only with `toolkit rule add` or `toolkit rule update`, after the owner says so.

## Git

- Keep commit messages under 50 characters. (2026-09-29, Mike Rihm, in chat)

## Replies

- Always show status as a table. (2026-09-29, Mike Rihm, in chat)
# Write Artifacts in Plain English

An artifact is something an agent generates for a person to look at: a
diagram, a chart, a dashboard, a visualization, a mockup, a slide deck, a
published page, or a generated document. This rule is about the words inside
one: the title, the headings, the labels, the notes, the captions, the body
text.

The project's output style says how the agent talks in chat. The words inside
an artifact follow the same style. This rule exists because the output style
reaches only the main chat: a helper agent, a skill, or a Codex session that
makes an artifact never sees it. Read the active style file when there is
one. Where this rule and that file differ, the style file wins.

## Write about the subject

Every word describes the thing the artifact shows. The reader opened it to
learn about that thing, not about the artifact or the conversation that
produced it.

- Do not narrate the artifact. "Here is where the change lands, but only the
  key pieces" says nothing about the system. Cut it, or say what changed.
- Do not tell the reader what matters. "Here is the load-bearing decision"
  tells them how to feel. Write the decision.
- Bring in the conversation only when it is the fact. A quote earns its place
  when the exact words are what the reader needs, and then it says who said
  it and when. A quote the reader cannot place is noise.

## A heading names what is under it

A heading is a label, not a hook. It says what the reader is about to look
at, in the words of the subject.

The four headings below are an example: a page of options for who can see and
edit which projects in a team web app. The left column sells the section; the
right column names it.

| Written | Say instead |
|---|---|
| Three ways to build the team tree, pick one | Team structure options |
| One question decides the whole shape | Decision: can a team lead edit their own team's projects? |
| Four facts that rule out the most obvious answers | How team access works |
| What shape actually hands to a real person | Project visibility by role |

A number belongs in a heading when the number is the fact: "Three departments
share one role". "Three ways to build it" only counts the section below, and
the reader can count.

## Use the real name

Call a thing what the system calls it, every time. In that example the real
names are team structure, project visibility, sharing rule, admin access, and
permission group. The page used picture words instead: "shape" for the team
structure, "lever" for a setting, "leaks" for access people should not have,
"flows up" for a manager getting access to their team's projects. That is
figurative language, and it is not allowed. It makes the reader translate, and
a reader who does not know the system cannot.

A term the reader may not know gets a plain definition the first time it
appears. After that, the term is used unchanged.

A box or label carries the real name. Anything it needs to say about itself
is one plain line.

## Say the plain thing

Use the active output style inside the artifact. This artifact rule also requires:

- Common words. Short sentences. One idea each.
- No figurative or metaphorical language. No idioms, no jokes, no picture word
  standing in for a real thing.
- No preamble. Start with the content.
- No closing line that sums up or cheers.
- Fewer words, never fewer facts. Every number, name, date, and quotation
  stays exactly as it is.

## What this rule does not decide

How the artifact is laid out: how many boxes, what an arrow says, where a
note goes, whether there is a key. Every artifact is different, and the agent
making it decides. This rule decides the words.
# Prepare a Session Handoff

When the owner says he is clearing context or ending the session, or asks for a handoff, use the `handoff` skill, whatever the session's length. When the session is long and the next step is complex, offer a handoff. Use the `handoff` skill. Before the handoff, review the current focus (`toolkit memory focus`) and the memory criteria; update the focus, and save only authorized lasting memory, with the `memory-save` skill. Then write the prompt. Skip the offer for small edits and quick lookups.
# Work Safely in a Shared Repository

Other sessions edit this repository now. Before your first edit, run:

```
git worktree list
git status
git fetch origin && git log --oneline -10
```

- No remote (`git remote` prints nothing): skip `git fetch`, and never report a fetch failure as a blocker.
- An unknown worktree, moved branch, or change you did not make means other sessions are live. Do not fix it. Tell the owner.
- Code, rules, skills, hooks, settings: use your own worktree and branch (`git worktree add .claude/worktrees/<name> -b claude/<name>`). Exception: a one-file edit asked for directly.
- Documentation-only saves: open the `publish-docs` skill.
- In the shared primary checkout, never switch branches, reset, rebase, or stash.
- Never touch another session's branch or uncommitted work.
- Stage paths by name. Never `git add -A`, `git add .`, or `git commit -a`. Read the full staged diff.
- Never hand-edit a generated file.
- Before taking a sequential number, check every tracker folder, worktree, and the remote. On a later collision, renumber only your own.
- Land implementation by pull request, merged with the owner's approval. A standing merge instruction the owner gave for this project counts.
- Before a merge, compare `git diff --name-only <default-branch>...<branch>` with `git status` in the primary checkout. A file in both: stop, name it, ask the owner.
- After the merge, remove your worktree and branch.
# Local Work-Item Folders

This project tracks work in local folders under `.work-items/`. The folder is
Git-ignored, lives in the main checkout, and is shared by every worktree. It is
not backed up by Git: `toolkit export` is the backup.

## An item is found by its ID, not its path

- An item is a folder holding a record, `WORK-ITEM.md`, and `DESIGN.md` when a
  design exists. The frontmatter `id` (for example `WI-001`) is the item's
  identity. The folder name and the file name may change.
- Refer to items by ID everywhere. Find an item's files with
  `toolkit work show <id> --path`. Never guess a path.
- Create items only with `toolkit work new`. It takes the next ID under a lock,
  so parallel sessions never pick the same one. IDs are never reused.

## The owner may move folders, and the agent adapts

- The owner may move, rename, nest, or group item folders by hand. That is
  normal. `toolkit work sync` finds every item again by its ID; the session
  hooks and every `toolkit work` command run it. Report what moved and continue.
  Use the `work-organize` skill to reconcile anything the sync reports as
  missing or duplicated.
- A record inside another item's folder is that item's sub-item: its `parent`
  follows its location. A plain folder with no record is a group and changes no
  parent.
- `archive/` is a reserved group. Items there are hidden from the briefing and
  from `toolkit work next`.
- Never move, group, archive, or rename items on your own initiative. When the
  owner asks, use `toolkit work move <id> --under <id|group|archive|root>`.

## What the tracker ignores, and what it generates

- Ignored: `work-item-template/`, any folder whose name starts with `_` or `.`,
  and any record whose title is still `<Work item title>`.
- Generated by `toolkit work sync`: `DASHBOARD.md`. State kept by `toolkit work`:
  `.toolkit-state.json` (the ID-to-path map and the highest ID used). Never edit
  either by hand.
- Change frontmatter fields (stage, status, parent, waiting on, approvals) only
  with `toolkit work` commands. Body sections may be edited directly or with
  `toolkit work edit`; the hook checks the record after each edit.
- Keep any other files the owner put in an item folder.

  An item with waiting_on: owner continues with work-decide, whatever its stage.

Statuses:
  Backlog      Logged; requirements are still being worked out (stages 01-02).
  Ready        Requirements approved; work can start (stage 03).
  In Progress  The item is active (stages 04-11). It does not mean building has started.
  In Review    The result is in a pull request, being deployed, or being written into the specifications (stages 12-14).
  Done         The owner accepted the result. Set only by toolkit work finish.
  Cancelled    Work stopped without the result. Set only by toolkit work cancel.

Types:
  discovery               Finding out what is needed.
  solution-design         Designing how something gets built.
  build                   Producing a change. Needs approved requirements before stage 03.
  data-load               Loading or changing data. Needs approved requirements before stage 03.
  repository-maintenance  Keeping the repository in order.
  research                Answering a question with sources.
  task                    A small piece of work.
  bug                     Something that does not work as it should.
  enhancement             An improvement to something that works.
  Other lower-case words are allowed as types.

Priorities: urgent, high, medium, low. Waiting on: owner, agent, external: <who>, none. Delivery: agent-led, owner-led, not-offered.

Approval gates:
  Requirements approval: asked by work-requirements; recorded with toolkit work approve <id> --requirements --by <name>. build and data-load items cannot reach stage 03 or later without it. Sets stage 03 when the item is earlier.
  Design approval: asked by solution-design; recorded with toolkit work approve <id> --design --by <name>. The design stays proposed until the owner approves it.
  Result approval (stage 11): asked by work-check; recorded with toolkit work approve <id> --result --by <name>. The owner approves the result before it is finished.
  Done: asked by work-finish; recorded with toolkit work finish <id> --by <name> --evidence <text> [--quote <owner's words>]. Only this command sets Done. With no recorded result approval it needs --quote, the owner's own words approving the result, and records that approval.
  Cancel: asked by work-finish; recorded with toolkit work cancel <id> --reason <text>. Only this command sets Cancelled. The reason is the owner's words.
  Delivery offer and team: asked by work-delegate; recorded with toolkit work set <id> --delivery agent-led|owner-led. Offered once per goal; the detail goes in Notes > Decisions and context.
  Project-wide decision: asked by work-decide; recorded with toolkit decision add --decision <text> --why <text> --by <name>. A row in DECISIONS.md at the project root.

What counts as approval:
  - Only the owner's explicit words count as approval. Quote them in the record.
  - A question, a suggestion, a tentative answer, or a saved draft is not approval.
  - Approval never covers merge, deployment, spending, or publishing.
  - Approval survives later stages. A stage alone does not prove approval: check the approval field.
  - A hand change that skips a gate is kept and reported as a question for the owner. It is never reverted.

Rules:
  - Status follows stage: 01-02 Backlog, 03 Ready, 04-11 In Progress, 12-14 In Review.
  - Stages may be skipped, repeated, and revisited. Record a one-line reason when a move is not obvious.
  - Pull-request stages (12) apply only to repository work.
  - Blocking is waiting_on plus the Overview Blockers line, never a status.
  - An item waiting on the owner continues with work-decide, whatever its stage.
  - An item that breaks an approval gate continues with work-decide until the owner answers.
  - An item at 11 User approval whose result approval is recorded continues with work-finish.
  - A Done or Cancelled item continues with nothing: it is finished. Reopen it with toolkit work set <id> --stage <s> --reopen.

# WI-001: Build the late fee command

## Overview

**Goal:** Provide a late fee command that reports the fee and total due in dollars.

**Current position:** The dollar command is built and tested on commit 3b2bc38. Five automated tests passed. An independent checker found R-01 and R-02 met on that commit. WI-002 remains the separate cents extension.

**Next action:** Mike reviews and approves the WI-001 dollar command result. The branch stays unmerged under his instruction.

**Blockers:** Result approval from Mike Rihm; merge is withheld.

**Related items:** WI-002 adds the --cents option under R-03.

## Roadmap

A phase is complete when its tasks are complete and its exit result has been checked.

| Phase | Outcome | Status | Exit result | Sub-items |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 — Dollar fee and total | The command prints the late fee and total due in dollars. | Done | R-01 and R-02 acceptance checks pass. | None. |
| P2 — Cents extension | WI-002 adds the optional cents line after the dollar command. | Not Started | WI-002 passes its R-03 acceptance checks. | WI-002 |

  **Done when:** The specified 200/10 and 1/2 outputs are exact, and invalid input exits unsuccessfully with empty stdout.  
  **Depends on:** None.
- [x] **P1-T02 — Verify the command** · Done  
  **Work:** Add a WI-001 test plan and run checks for rounding, valid spellings, large integers, and malformed arguments from the design Build and verification plan.  
  **Deliverable:** The WI-001 test plan, executable checks, and recorded results.  
  **Done when:** Every WI-001 acceptance check passes on the item branch and the result is ready for independent review.

## Requirements

**Overall status:** Finalized  
**Finalization rule:** Mark the overall requirements Finalized only when the agreed goal, every active requirement, and acceptance have been reviewed and approved by the owner. Record who approved them and when.

### Starting request

I want the late fee command built. When I run node bin/feecalc.js 200 --days 10 it should print "Late fee: $5.00  Total due: $205.00". The fee is 0.25% of the invoice amount for each day late. I also want a --cents option that adds a second line with the total due in whole cents, like "Total due in cents: 20500", because that is what our billing API takes. Do not build anything until I approve the requirements.

### Agreed goal

Provide a command that calculates a 0.25% daily late fee on an invoice and prints the late fee and total due in dollars. WI-002 delivers the separately requested --cents option under R-03.

### Active requirements

#### R-01 — Calculate the late fee

**Status:** Finalized  
**Applies to:** An overdue invoice amount and the number of days late supplied to the command.  
**Required behavior:** Calculate the late fee as 0.25% of the original invoice amount for each day late. Round the fee to the nearest cent, with half a cent rounded up. The total due is the invoice amount plus that rounded fee.  
**Boundaries and exceptions:** Valid invoice amounts are $0 or more with at most two decimal places. Valid day counts are whole numbers of 0 or more. Missing or invalid inputs do not produce a calculated total.  
**Acceptance check:** For an invoice amount of $200 and 10 days late, the fee is $5.00 and the total due is $205.00. For an invoice amount of $1 and 2 days late, the half-cent fee rounds up to $0.01 and the total due is $1.01. A missing or invalid amount or day count produces no calculated total.  
**Decision record:** Mike Rihm, 2026-09-29, starting request, rounding answer, input rule answer, missing or invalid input answer, total due answer, and approval of WI-001 requirements.  
**Open questions:** None.

#### R-02 — Print the dollar amounts

**Status:** Finalized  
**Applies to:** A command run with an invoice amount and the days-late option.  
**Required behavior:** For valid input, print one line containing the late fee and total due in dollars, each with two decimal places. For missing or invalid input, print a clear error to standard error, exit unsuccessfully, and print no total.  
**Boundaries and exceptions:** No second line is requested unless the cents option is supplied.  
**Acceptance check:** For an invoice amount of $200 and 10 days late, the first line is exactly "Late fee: $5.00  Total due: $205.00". A run with a missing or invalid input prints a clear error on standard error, exits unsuccessfully, and prints no total.  
**Decision record:** Mike Rihm, 2026-09-29, starting request, missing or invalid input answer, and approval of WI-001 requirements.  
**Open questions:** None.

#### R-03 — Print total due in cents on request

**Status:** Finalized  
**Applies to:** A command run with the cents option.  
**Required behavior:** Add a second line with the total due as a whole number of cents for the billing API.  
**Boundaries and exceptions:** The cents value must represent the invoice amount plus the rounded fee, matching the total due shown in dollars.  
**Acceptance check:** For an invoice amount of $200 and 10 days late, the cents option adds the line "Total due in cents: 20500" after the dollar line. For an invoice amount of $1 and 2 days late, it adds "Total due in cents: 101".  
**Decision record:** Mike Rihm, 2026-09-29, starting request, rounding answer, total due answer, and approval of WI-001 requirements.  
**Open questions:** None.

### Acceptance

This work item can be accepted when:

1. Running node bin/feecalc.js 200 --days 10 prints exactly "Late fee: $5.00  Total due: $205.00" (R-01, R-02).
2. Running the command with a missing or invalid input prints a clear error on standard error, exits unsuccessfully, and prints no total (R-01, R-02).
3. The dollar command correctly rounds a half-cent fee up once and adds the rounded fee to the invoice amount (R-01).
4. The owner approves the dollar command result. WI-002 has separate acceptance for the optional --cents output (R-03).

## Notes

### Decisions and context

- Mike Rihm approved R-01 to R-03 on 2026-09-29.
- Mike Rihm approved Option A on 2026-09-29 and instructed that --cents become sub-item WI-002 before any build. WI-001 directly builds only R-01 and R-02; WI-002 covers R-03 and has separate acceptance.
- Design approach: use built-in Node.js features and exact integer-cent arithmetic. The approved design records the split.
- The earlier design review passed independent critique before this scope split. No implementation had started.
- **Owner-led delivery (WI-001 goal: dollar fee and total):** Mike Rihm declined an agent team on 2026-09-29. This chat builds WI-001 without helpers. Git worktree, branch, and commits are approved for WI-001; merge is withheld pending owner approval.

### Resume here

WI-001 dollar command is built and tested at commit 3b2bc38 on branch claude/wi-001-build-the-late-fee-command. Five tests passed, and the independent checker reported R-01 and R-02 met on that commit. Await Mike result approval at stage 11. Do not merge until Mike explicitly authorizes it. WI-002 adds --cents later on its own item.

### Solution options and considerations

These are possibilities to evaluate, not approved requirements or design decisions.

- **For R-01:** Parse the amount into integer cents and calculate with exact integer arithmetic so accepted large values keep the correct cents.
- **For R-02 and R-03:** Use one Node.js command file and print the cents line only when requested.
